questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: A mineral estate held in trust
questions.learningObjective: Explain how minerals stayed tribal while the surface was allotted
questions.stem: The planner is asked how a mineral estate could remain tribal while the surface above it had already been allotted to individual families. Explain how that arrangement worked.

answer.exemplar: The statute divided the surface into allotments but reserved the oil, gas and other minerals beneath them to the tribe as a whole, so the producing estate was never divided among the individual allottees. The United States held that reserved estate in trust for the tribe, the tribal council exercised the power to lease it and to receive the royalties, and the net proceeds were then paid out to the heads who held the lease rights.

questions.explanation: The exemplar must distinguish the allotted surface from the reserved minerals that stayed tribal and in trust. Selling the minerals outright misses the trust.
questions.hint: Separate the surface from what lay beneath it.

answer.exemplar: The statute made the allotment and the citizenship operate as a single bargain rather than as two separate reforms. questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why the treaty system stopped
questions.learningObjective: Explain why federal treaty-making stopped and never resumed
questions.stem: The planner has to explain why the government stopped making treaties with the tribes and never resumed that practice.

answer.exemplar: Several things ended the treaty system. Congress ceased to make treaties in 1871 and withheld the treaty power from the executive, so the older practice of negotiated agreements ended in law. At the same time the government consolidated the tribes onto smaller reservations and then broke up the remaining land through allotment, and it claimed the right to change the terms of existing agreements by unilateral act, so treaties ceased to be the operative instrument for Indian land and status.

questions.explanation: The exemplar must name the statutory end of treaty-making and connect it to reservation consolidation and allotment. Blaming only tribal refusal leaves out the legal changes.
questions.hint: Include both the legal bar and the change in land tenure.

questions.topic: The statute that reversed allotment
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the 1934 statute reversed allotment
questions.stem: The planner must explain how the statute of 1934 reversed the allotment system that had been running since 1887.

answer.exemplar: The statute attacked allotment in several ways at once. It repealed the laws that had required allotment and had authorised the sale of the surplus lands, so no further parcels were carved out of the common estate. It restored to the tribes and to their members the lands and mineral rights acquired under the repealed acts and required the surplus to be brought back into trust. It also set out a national policy of tribal self-government and limited the further alienation of trust land by requiring the consent of the tribe.

questions.explanation: The exemplar must name the repeal, the restoration of land and mineral rights, and the new policy of self-government. Saying only that the law was kinder misses the machinery.
questions.hint: Name the repeal, the restoration and the consent rule.

questions.stem: A memo summary lists the effects of the 1934 statute. Which entry is accurate?

options.text: It required the surplus lands restored to the tribes in trust and barred alienation without tribal consent.
It permitted the Secretary to alienate tribal land without consent whenever it was wanted for a public use.
options.misconception: Recites narrow exceptions as if they were the general rule

options.text: It required every tribe to adopt a written constitution and corporate charter within five years.
options.misconception: Attributes a charter deadline the statute did not impose

options.text: It dissolved the tribal councils of the Five Tribes and put their lands under federal trusteeship.
options.misconception: Describes a measure aimed at restoring self-government

questions.explanation: The statute required the surplus to be restored in trust and limited alienation of trust land by requiring tribal consent, with narrow exceptions. A charter deadline was not imposed.
questions.hint: Look for the entry naming restoration and consent.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why the treaty system stopped
questions.learningObjective: Sequence the steps by which treaty-making ended
questions.stem: A memo records the stages by which the older practice of treaties with the tribes came to an end. Which order is correct?

options.text: Land is promised, tribes are consolidated, Congress ends treaty-making, and allotment breaks up the land.
Congress ends treaty-making, land is promised, tribes are consolidated, and allotment breaks up the land.
options.misconception: Puts the end of treaty-making before the agreements

options.text: Land is promised, Congress ends treaty-making, allotment breaks up the land, and tribes are consolidated.
options.misconception: Puts allotment before the consolidation of the reservations

options.text: Tribes are consolidated, land is promised, Congress ends treaty-making, and allotment breaks up the land.
options.misconception: Puts consolidation before the agreements that made it

questions.explanation: Agreements came first, consolidation followed, Congress ended treaty-making in 1871, and allotment finally broke up the land. Every other ordering starts with a later step.
questions.hint: Agreements, consolidation, the bar, then allotment.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: An office's own report against its own policy
questions.learningObjective: Identify the measure an agency proposed for judging its own success

stimulus.body: From the annual report of the office in charge of the schools: 'The education of Indian children is the most important branch of the service. It is designed to fit them for the settled life of the country, and the measure of its success will be the number of pupils who take up occupations in the country of their birth when they leave the school.'

questions.stem: The statement above defines how the office proposed to judge its own success. Which measure does it name?

options.text: The number of former pupils who took up occupations in their home country after leaving school.
The total enrolment of the schools during the year, without regard to what followed.
options.misconception: Takes the enrolment rather than the stated measure

options.text: The number of pupils whose families wrote letters of thanks to the office.
options.misconception: Invents a gratitude count as the measure

options.text: The number of teachers employed and the buildings erected for the schools.
options.misconception: Uses institutional growth as the measure of success

questions.explanation: The office names the number of pupils who took up occupations in their home country, an outcome measured after leaving rather than a count of those taught. Enrolment is not the measure.
questions.hint: Look for the outcome measured after the pupils left.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Citizenship written into a land statute
questions.learningObjective: Identify the conditions a land statute attached to allotment and trust

stimulus.body: Extract from a land statute: 'The patents for the allotments shall be issued in the name of the allottee, who shall be a citizen of the United States, and the United States shall hold the lands not so allotted in trust for the use of the tribe for the period of twenty-five years from the passage of this act, and if the tribe shall so elect, the trust shall continue for the use of said tribe.' A note records that the trust period was later extended.

questions.stem: Under the extract above, what conditions governed the allotment and the undivided land?

options.text: The allottee had to be a citizen, while the undivided land stayed in federal trust for a stated period.
The allottee did not need citizenship, and the undivided land passed at once to the states.
options.misconception: Drops the citizenship condition and invents a state transfer

options.text: The undivided land was held in trust only until the last patent issued, after which it was sold.
options.misconception: Shortens the trust term and invents a sale

options.text: Citizenship was required of the tribe as a whole before any patent could issue.
options.misconception: Turns an individual condition into a tribal one

questions.explanation: The extract makes citizenship the condition of the patent and keeps the undivided land in trust for a fixed term the tribe could extend. Ending the trust at the last patent contradicts it.
questions.hint: Note the condition and the length of the trust.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: A mineral estate held in trust
questions.learningObjective: Combine head right figures with the terms of the mineral trust
questions.stem: A memo table records that 1,000 heads held leasehold interests in a tribal trust, and the year's net royalties of 400,000 dollars were shared among them. Which conclusion best combines the table with the terms of the trust?

options.text: The undivided estate was held in trust and its earnings divided among the heads whose leases it protected.
The 1,000 heads each owned a separate share of the mineral estate, which the trust merely administered.
options.misconception: Turns head rights into a division of the mineral estate

options.text: The royalties were paid out because the trust had already been dissolved by the government.
options.misconception: Invents a dissolution of the trust

options.text: The payments show that the tribe had leased the estate outright with no trust remaining.
options.misconception: Reads royalty payments as a completed sale

questions.explanation: A royalty paid to the heads under the trust shows an undivided estate whose earnings went to the heads whose lease rights it protected. Individual ownership of the minerals contradicts this.
questions.hint: Ask what the payment proves about ownership of the estate.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: The statute that reversed allotment
questions.learningObjective: Compute the acreage a tribe held in trust after restoration
questions.stem: One tribe in the memo had 512,000 acres allotted and 128,000 acres opened to settlement before the statute of 1934. Stage one, state what the statute required to happen to that surplus; stage two, compute the acreage the tribe would hold in trust afterwards.

options.text: The surplus had to be restored to the tribe in trust, giving the tribe 128,000 acres in trust.
The surplus had to be restored to the tribe in trust, giving the tribe 640,000 acres in trust.
options.misconception: Adds the allotted acreage to the restored surplus

options.text: The surplus could stay open to settlement, so the tribe would hold no acres in trust.
options.misconception: Ignores the restoration required by the statute

options.text: The surplus had to be restored to the tribe in trust, giving the tribe 384,000 acres in trust.
options.misconception: Subtracts the surplus from the allotted acreage

questions.explanation: The statute required the surplus to be restored in trust, and the table shows the surplus as 128,000 acres. Adding the allotted acres to it misreads the table.
questions.hint: Restored acreage is the surplus, not the sum or difference

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why the treaty system stopped
questions.learningObjective: Draw a conclusion about treaties from the later agreement practice
questions.stem: A memo describes how the government fixed the boundary of a reservation by agreement with the people who lived there. Which conclusion about the treaty system follows?

options.text: The government kept using agreements to fix lines while making no new treaties, so the old system narrowed.
The government had already abandoned agreements entirely by the time the boundaries were fixed.
options.misconception: Claims agreement stopped before the boundaries were set

options.text: The agreements were made because the tribes had won control of the treaty-making power.
options.misconception: Invents a transfer of the treaty power to the tribes

options.text: The boundaries were fixed without the tribes' involvement, which shows the agreements were sham.
options.misconception: Contradicts an agreement described as joint

questions.explanation: Using agreements to fix lines while making no new treaties narrows the old system to a limited practice. Saying agreement had already ended misreads the memo.
questions.hint: Weigh the agreements against the absence of new treaties.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: An office's own report against its own policy
questions.learningObjective: Compute the change in reported cost per pupil over time
questions.stem: The office's reported cost for each pupil is tabulated for four years: 148 dollars in 1875, 213 in 1880, 287 in 1885 and 374 in 1890. By how much did the reported cost per pupil rise between 1875 and 1890?

options.text: Exactly 8 children could be schooled for the cost of one prisoner's year.
About 192 children could be schooled for the cost of one prisoner's year.
options.misconception: Subtracts the year from the cost instead of the costs

options.text: About 24 children could be schooled for the cost of one prisoner's year.
options.misconception: Reverses the direction of the change

options.text: About 168 children could be schooled for the cost of one prisoner's year.
options.misconception: Adds the two figures rather than subtracting them

questions.explanation: Subtracting the earliest figure from the latest gives 374 minus 148, which is 226 dollars for each pupil. Adding the two figures instead of subtracting them does not fit.
questions.hint: Subtract the earliest figure from the latest.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Citizenship written into a land statute
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a land statute attached citizenship to the granting of an allotment
questions.stem: The planner is asked why the makers of a land statute attached citizenship to the granting of an allotment.

answer.exemplar: The makers wanted the allotment and the citizenship to operate together as a single bargain rather than as separate reforms. A patent in severalty was a grant of private land, and the government was willing to make that grant only to a person who had become a citizen of the United States and had given up the rights that came with membership in the tribe. In exchange, the undivided residue of the tribal estate was left with the United States as trustee, so the surface was individualised while the remainder stayed under federal control.

questions.explanation: The exemplar must connect the citizenship condition to the patent and to the trust over the undivided residue. Treating citizenship as a moral add-on misses the exchange.
questions.hint: Describe the exchange the statute proposed.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: A mineral estate held in trust
questions.learningObjective: Identify an accurate feature of the trusteeship of a mineral estate
questions.stem: A memo summary lists features of the trusteeship of a mineral estate. Which entry is accurate?

options.text: The council granted the leases, the United States collected the rents, and the net proceeds went to the heads.
The United States chose the lessees and paid the proceeds to the shareholders as owners of the estate.
options.misconception: Makes the United States the lessor and the heads the owners

options.text: The trusteeship ended when the last patent was issued, returning the minerals to the tribe in fee simple.
options.misconception: Ends the trust at the issuance of the last patent

options.text: The trusteeship existed only so that the government could collect the royalties for its own revenue.
options.misconception: Describes the trust as a revenue device

questions.explanation: The council leased, the United States collected and the heads received the net proceeds, which is how the trusteeship operated. Making the government the lessor contradicts that.
questions.hint: Look for the entry splitting council, trustee and recipients

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: The statute that reversed allotment
questions.learningObjective: Sequence the stages of returning land to tribal trust
questions.stem: A memo lists the stages by which land was brought back into tribal trust after the allotment system ended. Which sequence is correct?

options.text: Allotment laws are repealed, surplus and mineral rights restored, and further sales need tribal consent.
The surplus is restored, allotment repealed, further sales need no consent, and the lands are held in trust.
options.misconception: Puts the restoration before the repeal that authorised it

options.text: Allotment laws are repealed, sales need no consent, the surplus is restored, and the lands are held in trust.
options.misconception: Allows sales without consent, which the statute restricted

options.text: Further sales need consent, allotment repealed, the surplus is restored, and the lands are held in trust.
options.misconception: Puts the consent rule before the repeal that created it

questions.explanation: Repeal came first, then the restoration of the surplus and mineral rights, then the consent rule for further sales, with the lands in trust throughout. Consent before repeal inverts the sequence.
questions.hint: Repeal, restoration, consent, trust.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why the treaty system stopped
questions.learningObjective: Identify what happened to treaty-making in the administration's own account

stimulus.body: From the report of a federal official sent to settle matters with the tribes: 'We were directed to inform the parties that no further treaties would be made with them, and that the terms of their existing agreements would be settled by the officers of the government in the manner provided by law. The people received the information with dissatisfaction, but the instructions of the department were followed.'

questions.stem: The report above shows what happened to treaty-making in practice. Which reading is correct?

options.text: Federal officers told the tribes that no new treaties would be made, and old agreements were settled by them.
Federal officers negotiated new treaties with the tribes but were refused by the people they met.
options.misconception: Reads a refusal of the terms as a refusal to negotiate

options.text: The department instructed its officers to restore the earlier agreements in full at once.
options.misconception: Claims the department restored the agreements it had ended

options.text: The tribes accepted the change without dissatisfaction, as the report records.
options.misconception: Contradicts the report's own statement of dissatisfaction

questions.explanation: The report describes officers telling the tribes that no further treaties would be made and that existing agreements would be settled by officers. A contented reception contradicts the record.
questions.hint: Weigh each option against the officer's plain account.
